blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two strings haystack and needle, return the index of the first occurrence of needle inside haystack, or -1 if needle never appears at all.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding a Short Phrase Inside a Long Paragraph
blocks.text: Like scanning a long paragraph of text for the first place a specific short phrase appears, checking every possible starting point until a full match is found or the paragraph runs out.

blocks.caption: Find the first starting position in haystack where needle matches exactly

blocks.text: Edge case: needle equals haystack exactly
When needle is identical to the entire haystack, it matches starting at the very first position, giving 0.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask what a failed character by character comparison actually leaves behind, and whether that work can be reused instead of discarded.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force compares needle against haystack character by character at every position, but a mismatch throws away all the partial matching work done so far, gaining nothing to speed up the next attempt.

Observation 2: Instead of comparing characters directly at every position, each window of haystack could be summarized by a single number, a hash, so that most non matching positions could be ruled out with one cheap numeric comparison instead of scanning up to m characters.

Observation 3: Computing that hash from scratch for every window would be just as slow as the brute force, so the real trick is a rolling hash, updating the previous window's hash in constant time by removing the outgoing character's contribution and adding the incoming character's contribution.

Observation 4: Because two different windows can occasionally hash to the same value by pure coincidence, every hash match still requires a direct character comparison to confirm a true match, illustrated concretely by tracing haystack equal to "leetcode" against needle equal to "leeto", where two different windows, "etcod" and "tcode", happen to share the exact same simple additive hash despite being different strings, proving why verification can never be skipped.

Recognizing that a rolling hash can summarize each window in constant time, but a hash match is only a candidate that still needs direct verification, is what turns character by character scanning into an average case linear time search.
6. Brute Force Solution
Try every possible starting position in haystack, and at each one, compare needle against haystack character by character to check for a full match.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting position i in haystack where needle could still fit, compare needle to haystack starting at i, character by character.
If every character matches, return i.
If no starting position produces a full match, return -1.

codes.python:
def str_str(haystack, needle):
    n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)
    for i in range(n - m + 1):                               # every position where needle could still fit
        if haystack[i:i + m] == needle:                          # compare character by character
            return i
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    haystack = "sadbutsad"
    needle = "sad"
    print(str_str(haystack, needle))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop only tries starting positions where needle could still physically fit within the remaining length of haystack.
A direct substring comparison at each position checks every character in one step, returning immediately the moment a full match is found.
Returning -1 after the loop correctly signals that no valid starting position produced a complete match.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible starting position is checked for a full match, so the first true occurrence is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m) in the worst case, comparing up to m characters at each of roughly n starting positions.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the substring comparisons themselves.
Limitation: a failed comparison at one starting position throws away all of the character matching work already done, instead of reusing it to help skip ahead faster.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: every position starts its comparison completely from scratch, discarding all information from the previous position's failed attempt.

What summarizing each window as a single hash fixes: comparing two numbers is far cheaper than comparing m characters, ruling out most positions with a single cheap check.

What rolling the hash forward fixes on top of that: updating the previous hash in constant time, instead of recomputing it from scratch, keeps the per-position cost constant rather than proportional to m.

The core idea: roll the hash forward one position at a time, and whenever it matches needle's hash, confirm the match with one direct character by character comparison to rule out a coincidental collision.

Use a rolling hash (the Rabin-Karp technique): compute a hash value for needle once, then compute the hash of the first window of haystack of the same length. As the window slides one position at a time, update its hash in constant time using a rolling formula, instead of rehashing the whole window from scratch. Whenever a window's hash matches needle's hash, do a direct character by character comparison to confirm it is a true match and not just a hash collision.
9. Optimized Solution
Compute a rolling hash for each window of haystack and compare it against needle's hash, confirming true matches with a direct comparison.
Dry run for haystack = "leetcode", needle = "leeto" (using a simple additive hash of character codes, for illustration only)

blocks.caption: Optimized: a rolling hash lets each window's hash update in constant time as it slides

codes.python:
def str_str(haystack, needle):
    n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)
    if m == 0:
        return 0
    base, mod = 256, 1_000_000_007
    high_power = pow(base, m - 1, mod)

    needle_hash = 0
    window_hash = 0
    for i in range(m):
        needle_hash = (needle_hash * base + ord(needle[i])) % mod
        window_hash = (window_hash * base + ord(haystack[i])) % mod

    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if window_hash == needle_hash and haystack[i:i + m] == needle:  # verify to rule out a hash collision
            return i
        if i + m < n:
            window_hash = (window_hash - ord(haystack[i]) * high_power) % mod
            window_hash = (window_hash * base + ord(haystack[i + m])) % mod   # roll the window forward
            window_hash %= mod
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    haystack = "sadbutsad"
    needle = "sad"
    print(str_str(haystack, needle))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the rolling update always produces the exact hash of the current window in constant time, so comparing it against needle's hash correctly identifies every position worth a direct character comparison, and skips every position whose hash provably differs, without ever needing to rescan the window's actual characters just to compute its hash.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A window's hash does not match needle's hash","The position is ruled out immediately with no character comparison at all","Most non matching positions are skipped extremely cheaply"],["A window's hash does match needle's hash","A direct character by character comparison confirms whether this is a true match or just a coincidental hash collision","The final answer is never wrong, even though the hash comparison alone is not fully reliable"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus m) on average, since each window's hash updates in constant time. Worst case remains O(n times m) if hash collisions force many direct verifications.
Space: O(1) extra, only a few rolling hash values are kept.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Rabin-Karp trades a small risk of hash collisions for the ability to compare an entire window against needle in constant time on average, and the same rolling hash idea generalizes directly to searching for many different patterns at once.
Common Mistakes

items: Skipping the direct character comparison after a hash match, which risks accepting a false positive caused by a hash collision.
Recomputing each window's hash from scratch instead of rolling it forward, which throws away the whole benefit of the technique.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An empty needle","By convention matches at index 0 immediately."],["A needle longer than haystack","Can never match and should return -1 right away."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention that a separate, guaranteed worst case linear algorithm exists too, the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, which avoids the hash collision risk entirely by precomputing how far a failed match can safely skip ahead, at the cost of a more involved preprocessing step.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you guarantee worst case linear time", think: Knuth-Morris-Pratt, which precomputes skip distances instead of relying on hashing.
If the interviewer says "what if two windows hash the same by coincidence", think: always confirm a hash match with a direct character comparison before accepting it.
If the interviewer says "can you search for many patterns at once", think: the same rolling hash idea extends directly, computing one hash per pattern and checking each window against all of them.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why must a hash match always be confirmed with a direct character comparison?
How does the rolling hash formula avoid recomputing the entire window's hash from scratch?
How would you extend this approach to search for multiple different needles at once within the same haystack?
Why does Knuth-Morris-Pratt guarantee worst case linear time while Rabin-Karp does not?
How would you choose the base and modulus values to minimize the chance of hash collisions in practice?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Repeated Substring Pattern, Repeated String Match, Longest Happy Prefix, and other later string matching problems in this sheet, which build directly on the same rolling hash or prefix function ideas introduced here.
Longest Common Prefix, whose single running candidate avoided repeated pairwise comparison, a related "reuse prior work instead of recomputing" instinct applied here to hashing entire windows.
Any "find a pattern inside a larger text" problem, where a rolling hash or a precomputed skip table (as in Knuth-Morris-Pratt) is the standard way to beat naive character by character scanning.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times m) time, O(1) extra space. Optimized (Rabin-Karp rolling hash): O(n plus m) time on average, O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Rabin-Karp rolling hash, summarizing each window with a number that updates in constant time as it slides.

Core Idea: rolling a window's hash forward in constant time lets most positions be ruled out with a single numeric comparison, but every hash match still needs a direct character comparison to rule out a coincidental collision.
Time: O(n times m) for the brute force, O(n plus m) on average for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: a hash match is a candidate, never a proof, so verification by direct comparison is a mandatory step, not an optional safeguard.
Interview Difficulty: the rolling hash formula itself is the tricky part to get exactly right; forgetting the verification step is the most common way this approach silently produces wrong answers.
One line memory trick: roll the hash forward in constant time, and always verify a hash match with a real comparison.
